notes.meaning: Jeremiah finished speaking every word the Lord had given him for the people. He did not add his own ideas or hold anything back. True messengers of God deliver only what God commands them to say.

Azariah, Johanan, and the other proud leaders accused Jeremiah of lying. Their pride made them reject God's guidance because it went against what they had already decided to do. Instead of admitting they wanted their own way, they claimed the Lord had never sent the prophet.

The leaders blamed Baruch, Jeremiah's secretary, claiming he was turning the prophet against them. They made up the excuse that Baruch wanted the Babylonians to capture or kill them. When people want to keep sinning, they often make false charges against godly people rather than face the truth.

Johanan and his army officers refused to obey the Lord's command to stay in Judah. Earlier they had promised to follow God's direction whether it seemed good or bad. Now they broke their word because trusting God felt riskier to them than running to Egypt.

The leaders gathered up all the remaining people of Judah, including the king's daughters and refugees who had returned from neighboring lands. They also forced Jeremiah and Baruch to go with them against their will. The faithful prophet and his scribe were carried off like prisoners by their own people.

The group crossed the border into Egypt in direct rebellion against God's word. They stopped at Tahpanhes, a frontier city that guarded the entrance into the country. By fleeing back to Egypt, they turned away from God's protection and returned to the land that had once enslaved their ancestors.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An early church tradition recorded by Tertullian and Jerome holds that Jeremiah was stoned to death at Tahpanhes by his rebellious countrymen.

notes.meaning: Even though Jeremiah was now in a foreign land, the Lord spoke to him at Tahpanhes. God's presence and His word could not be kept out by borders. The refugees could run away from Judah, but they could not get away from God.

God told Jeremiah to take large stones and bury them in the mortar of the brick pavement near Pharaoh's palace. He had to do this in plain view of the men of Judah. This acted sign showed that a foreign conqueror would soon set his throne right on that spot.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists in the late nineteenth century uncovered a large raised brick platform outside the palace fort at Tell Defenneh (ancient Tahpanhes), which many scholars identify as the pavement described here.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah explained the sign to the people: the Lord would bring King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to Egypt. God calls Nebuchadnezzar His servant because the king would carry out God's plan, even without realizing it. Nebuchadnezzar would set his royal throne and canopy right above the stones Jeremiah had hidden.

Nebuchadnezzar would invade Egypt and bring judgment upon it. Some people would die of disease or starvation, others would be killed in battle, and others would be carried away as prisoners. The refugees who ran to Egypt to escape Babylon would find that God's judgment caught up with them there.

The invader would set fire to the temples of Egypt, burn their wooden idols, and take their metal statues away as plunder. Nebuchadnezzar would take over Egypt as easily as a shepherd wraps his cloak around himself, leaving the country unharmed and loaded with treasure. This proved that Egypt's false gods had no power to save anyone.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several modern Bible translations render the shepherd imagery as picking vermin or lice off a cloak, meaning Nebuchadnezzar would quickly strip Egypt bare.

notes.meaning: The Babylonians would tear down the stone obelisks at Beth-shemesh, the city known as the house of the sun, and burn down the Egyptian shrines. This center of sun worship was famous for its towering stone pillars. God would demonstrate that He alone is the true Lord by destroying the monuments of Egypt's greatest gods.
